The Poisson Distribution

Source: R/api-distributions.R
nv_poisson.Rd

Density (nv_dpois), distribution function (nv_ppois), and quantile function (nv_qpois) for the Poisson distribution with mean lambda.

Usage

nv_dpois(x, lambda, log = FALSE)

nv_ppois(q, lambda, lower_tail = TRUE, log_p = FALSE)

nv_qpois(p, lambda, lower_tail = TRUE, log_p = FALSE)

Arguments

x, q

(arrayish)
Quantiles at which to evaluate the density (x) or the distribution function (q). These are counts, given as integers or floats; see Non-Integer Values for values that are not whole numbers.

lambda

(arrayish)
Mean of the distribution. Scalars broadcast; otherwise lambda and x/q/p must have the same shape.

log, log_p

(logical(1))
If TRUE, the densities/probabilities are given as logarithms. For nv_qpois this describes the input p.

lower_tail

(logical(1))
If TRUE (default), probabilities are \(P(X \le x)\); otherwise, \(P(X > x)\).

p

(arrayish)
Probabilities at which to evaluate the quantile function. Values outside \([0, 1]\) give NaN. With log_p = TRUE, supply log-probabilities in \([-\infty, 0]\) instead.

Value

(arrayish)
nv_dpois(), nv_ppois(), and nv_qpois() return an arrayish with the float data type described under Data Types and the shape after scalar broadcasting with lambda.

Details

The Poisson distribution has probability mass function: $$p(x) = \frac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}, \quad x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$ where \(\lambda\) is lambda.

Invalid arguments give NaN, as in base R, but without a warning (that is a negative lambda). Zero and infinite lambda follow base R's endpoint conventions:

  • lambda = 0: the point mass at zero.

  • lambda = Inf: densities are zero. The lower-tail probability is zero at finite q and one at q = Inf. Quantiles are NaN.

nv_dpois uses the saddle point expansion of Loader (2000), as base R does. nv_ppois uses the incomplete gamma function methods of base R's stats::pgamma(): a series in the tails, and an asymptotic expansion where q and lambda are large and close. nv_qpois finds the smallest \(x\) with \(P(X \le x) \ge p\), starting from a Cornish-Fisher approximation as base R does. Above 2^24 in f32 and 2^53 in f64 not every whole number is a float, and nv_qpois then returns the smallest float \(x\) with \(P(X \le x) \ge p\).

Non-Integer Values

x and q are counts, but any value is accepted, and one that is not a whole number is treated as in base R, without its warnings:

  • nv_dpois() takes an x within a relative 1e-9 of a whole number, that is with \(|x - \mathrm{round}(x)| \le 10^{-9} \max(|x|, 1)\), as that whole number. Any other x has probability zero.

  • nv_ppois() rounds q down, except that a q within 1e-7 below a whole number counts as that number.

  • A negative x or q is below the support even where it is within the tolerance of zero: such an x has probability zero, and such a q has \(P(X \le q) = 0\).

Finite quantiles from nv_qpois() are always whole numbers. Since x and q are used only as whole numbers, their gradient is zero wherever a gradient can be taken.

Gradients

nv_dpois and nv_ppois can be differentiated with respect to lambda, to any order. At lambda = 0, where only a right derivative exists, the implementation returns it for nv_dpois(0, lambda) and, by convention, zero for the other probabilities at lambda = 0. nv_qpois is a step function, and autodiff returns a zero gradient for all of its arguments.

Data Types

nv_dpois(), nv_ppois() and nv_qpois() compute at a float data type and return it. If x/q/p is a float, they compute at its data type; an R double settles on the default float. An integer x/q/p (an array or an R integer) is converted to the widest float among the arrays given for lambda, or to the default float if there is none. Integers beyond \(2^{24}\) are not all exact at f32, so a large integer may change in that conversion.

An R value for lambda takes the computing data type. An array is promoted to it, so a wider one (e.g. f64 for an f32 x) is an error.

References

Loader C (2000). “Fast and Accurate Computation of Binomial Probabilities.” https://www.r-project.org/doc/reports/CLoader-dbinom-2002.pdf.

Examples

x <- nv_array(c(0, 1, 2, 5, 10))
nv_dpois(x, lambda = 4)
#> AnvlArray
#>  0.0183
#>  0.0733
#>  0.1465
#>  0.1563
#>  0.0053
#> [ CPUf32{5} ] 
nv_dpois(x, lambda = 4, log = TRUE)
#> AnvlArray
#>  -4.0000
#>  -2.6137
#>  -1.9206
#>  -1.8560
#>  -5.2415
#> [ CPUf32{5} ] 

nv_ppois(x, lambda = 4)
#> AnvlArray
#>  0.0183
#>  0.0916
#>  0.2381
#>  0.7851
#>  0.9972
#> [ CPUf32{5} ] 
nv_ppois(x, lambda = 4, lower_tail = FALSE)
#> AnvlArray
#>  0.9817
#>  0.9084
#>  0.7619
#>  0.2149
#>  0.0028
#> [ CPUf32{5} ] 
nv_ppois(x, lambda = 4, log_p = TRUE)
#> AnvlArray
#>  -4.0000
#>  -2.3906
#>  -1.4351
#>  -0.2419
#>  -0.0028
#> [ CPUf32{5} ] 

p <- nv_array(c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
nv_qpois(p, lambda = 4)
#> AnvlArray
#>  1
#>  4
#>  8
#> [ CPUf32{3} ] 
nv_qpois(p, lambda = 4, lower_tail = FALSE)
#> AnvlArray
#>  8
#>  4
#>  1
#> [ CPUf32{3} ] 
nv_qpois(
  nv_array(c(-700, -2, -0.1), dtype = "f64"),
  lambda = 1000,
  log_p = TRUE
)
#> AnvlArray
#>    89
#>   965
#>  1042
#> [ CPUf64{3} ]
